conventions: TypeScript strict, ESM, Prettier via ESLint: 2 spaces, double quotes, trailing commas, 80 columns. `yarn test:code` runs with --max-warnings=0.
Type imports are separate `import type` statements (consistent-type-imports). Keep import/order: external and @excalidraw/* first, then parent, then sibling, then type imports.

Inside packages/element import siblings relatively (./textRanges). Inside packages/excalidraw import element code from "@excalidraw/element", types from "@excalidraw/element/types", and never through a packages/excalidraw barrel.
New DOM use goes through app.ownerDocument / app.ownerWindow, or the ownerDocument of a mounted node. Never use the global document in new code.
Prefer immutable data. Range arrays and range objects are never mutated in place: every change builds new objects (delta.ts compares entries by identity).
A style-only change goes through newElementWith or a spread, never through mutateElement: mutateElement keeps the same object, so elementWithCanvasCache would paint stale text.
New element fields get a JSDoc block in types.ts. Comments state why, not what, and stay short.

Tests run on Vitest with globals, jsdom and vitest-canvas-mock. Use API, UI, Keyboard, getTextEditor, updateTextEditor and act from the existing helpers. Assert with expect; no toMatchSnapshot and no new snapshot files anywhere.
In the test env getLineWidth returns text.length * 10, so x and width values in tests are exact multiples of 10.
UI strings go through t("labels.x") and live in packages/excalidraw/locales/en.json only. Every other locale file is Crowdin's.

decisions.choice: Run constraint: work only from this branch's code and the brief. Do not look at the upstream excalidraw repo, its PRs or issues, upstream/master or master, and do not base anything on them. This binds every phase and every model, the Gemini worker included.
decisions.reason: The person's Gate 0 answer, word for word.

decisions.choice: Concurrent edits: keep your reading of "survive" and do not narrow the brief to last-write-wins. The losing version's ranges are carried onto the winning text, no client shows stale offsets, all clients converge whichever order they receive versions in, and a removed range does not come back.
rejected: Last-write-wins on the whole element or on the textRanges key
decisions.reason: The person's Gate 0 answer.

decisions.choice: ExcalidrawTextElement gets one optional key `textRanges?: ExcalidrawTextRanges` = { textHash: number; ranges: ExcalidrawTextRange[] }. textHash is hashString(originalText). A range is { id, start, end, z, color?, highlight?, retired?, origin? }: start and end are half-open UTF-16 offsets into originalText; id is randomId() and encodes no user, client or device; z is the layer; color and highlight are a colour string (sets it), null (clears it) or absent (leaves it alone). id, z, color and highlight never change after a range is created. origin is { version, versionNonce, text, start, end }, or { version, versionNonce, textFrom, start, end } when another record of the same container holds that text, as One copy of each register text states.
rejected: Two top-level keys (ranges plus a tombstone list), which history would apply separately
One range per attribute with a kind field: FR-1 says colour and/or highlight on one range
decisions.reason: One replaced value keeps text offsets and their hash together. Anchoring to originalText means a re-wrap alone never changes offsets (FR-1).

decisions.topic: Key absent by default (FR-2 as revised at Gate 1)
decisions.choice: An element that has NEVER had ranges carries no textRanges key, in memory or on save: newTextElement does not set it, restore never adds it, and a colour or reset that changes no visible style leaves it absent. An element whose ranges were all removed keeps its textRanges container as the marker FR-19 needs: clear, retired and collapsed records stay in it.
decisions.reason: Keeps every existing snapshot and legacy file byte-identical, and gives a removal something to travel in.

decisions.topic: Layers: how one style is decided per character (FR-4)
decisions.choice: Ranges are layers, not disjoint segments. A style operation never rewrites an existing range's span: it adds one record on top with z = 1 + the highest z in the element. A colour pick adds { color } and touches nothing else, a highlight pick adds { highlight }, Reset adds { color: null, highlight: null }. A style with a null is a removal and also retires what it touches (see Removal and tombstones). For each attribute separately, the style of a character comes from the covering, non-retired record with that attribute present, ordered by highest z, then null before a string at equal z, then highest id. getTextStyleRuns is the only reader of this order and returns disjoint runs. Stored records of one attribute may overlap, because a style operation never shrinks a record.
rejected: Disjoint records with no clear on top: two clients each removing half of a range would keep each other's remainder, so the whole range would come back
Per-range revision counters: they cannot express a partial removal
decisions.reason: A grow-only set of immutable records is a join under union, which is what makes merging order-independent, and a partial removal survives because a clear is a record like any other.

decisions.choice: Text edits map offsets through diffText hunks. Insertion strictly inside a range extends it. Insertion exactly at a range's start shifts it and is not included. Insertion exactly at a range's end leaves it alone and is not included. A replacement overlapping a boundary leaves the inserted text outside the range. Deletion shrinks a range. A range whose characters are all deleted stays in the list collapsed (start === end) and native (no origin): it styles nothing from then on, and typing the same text again never reopens it, because mapStart(p) >= mapEnd(p) keeps a collapsed span collapsed. Its id is what stops a merge re-adding it from a peer's copy. Where repeated text lets an insertion or a deletion sit at a word edge and not inside the word, the final diff pass puts it at the edge, so these rules read it there.
rejected: Extending a range when typing at its end: it would also extend every clear, so typing after a removed word would change what was removed
Dropping a range whose characters are all deleted: a peer then holds an id the base does not, so the merge re-adds it with the old text in origin, and retyping the word turns it red again
decisions.reason: One rule for start and one for end, used by the editor, list markers, history and carrying, so a range and a clear over it always move together.

decisions.topic: Merged element's version and nonce (FR-19, FR-20, NFR-3)
decisions.choice: reconcileElements picks the base exactly as today (shouldDiscardRemoteElement is unchanged and still exported). The merged element is { ...base, textRanges: merged }: inside reconcileElements it keeps the base's version, versionNonce, updated and every other field. Both clients call mergeTextRanges(base = the same winner, other = the same loser), so two clients with the same two versions compute the same element (NFR-3). If the merged ranges equal the base's, the base object itself is returned. In the app, Collab._reconcileElements then runs bumpElementVersions(reconciled, existing) (Collab.tsx:790, unchanged). After reconcile it fires in one case only: the client took a remote element at an equal version with a different nonce. That element gets version + 1, a fresh random versionNonce and a new updated, and nothing else holds that version and nonce. So after an equal-version race the client whose own element won holds the winner's version and nonce, the client that took the remote holds the bumped ones, and the two are equal in every other field, originalText and textRanges included. A higher-version winner is not bumped, so in that race both clients match on every field at once. Nothing rebroadcasts at that moment: Collab sets lastBroadcastedOrReceivedSceneVersion from the bumped total, so broadcastElements sees nothing newer. The next delivery ends the difference: the receiver takes the higher version, the merge returns it unchanged, no bump fires because the local version is lower, and both clients match on every field. mergeTextRanges also runs when version and nonce are equal, so a client still holding the un-merged winner picks up the merged ranges from a full sync. Two clients that both took the remote in one race hold the same version with different nonces and equal content: their next exchange is an ordinary equal-version race, one bumps once more, and the delivery after that ends it, as for every element today.
rejected: Bumping the version inside the merge: two clients with the same two versions would compute different elements (NFR-3), and elements with no ranges must reconcile as today
Deriving a new nonce from a hash of the merged state: the nonce is the tie-break, so it would change the winner
decisions.reason: Base fields are a last-write-wins register and the range table is a union, and the product of two joins is a join: commutative, associative and idempotent, so arrival order cannot matter. Collab's bump sits outside that join and behaves like one more local version with the same content, so it delays field-for-field equality by one delivery and cannot change what clients converge to.

decisions.topic: Carrying ranges onto the winning text (FR-19)
decisions.choice: Each record has a position register, a value compared as (higher version, then lower versionNonce). A record's register is its `origin` field if present, with a textFrom read from the record it names, else { version, versionNonce, text: originalText, start, end } of the element holding it. If the base holds the id with no origin, the base's offsets win. Otherwise the newest register among the two sides is mapped onto the base's text through diffText(register.text, base.originalText, meter) and mapSpanThroughHunks, as the Diff budget decision states, and stored as the record's origin, unchanged but for where its text lives (One copy of each register text). The mapping always starts from the register's own text, never from an intermediate merged text, so carrying through any number of merges gives the same offsets as carrying directly. A carried record whose characters are gone in the base stays in the list collapsed (start === end) with its origin, because a later winning text may still hold them. Any local edit (a style op or a text edit) makes every record native again by dropping origin. A bump never touches origin. A native record on a bumped element takes the bumped version and nonce as its register, with the same text and offsets, so it maps to the same place: two clients can hold different origin fields for a record until the next delivery, the newer register wins that delivery, and their offsets agree throughout.
rejected: Common prefix and suffix only: when both ends of a text changed, everything in the middle would be lost
Mapping from the previous merged text: path-dependent once three versions race
Finding the styled substring by search: a word edited on the winning side would lose its range
decisions.reason: offsets = f(register, winning text) is a pure function of two joined values, which is the only way three-way races stay order-independent with no common ancestor.

decisions.choice: A removal of a selection (Reset, or the transparent highlight swatch) does three things. It retires, by id, every record it touches all of whose string attributes it clears, whether it covers that record fully or partly, so no text path can bring any of that record back. For a record it covers only partly, it adds the part outside the selection as a fresh record at the same z (a kept part). It adds a clear record on top, which hides every lower layer over that span, stays in the list, and is carried like any other record. Two clients each clearing part of a range hide all of it, because each one's kept part lies under the other's clear. A colour edit racing a removal at the same z loses to the removal. A range created at a higher z by a client that had not seen the removal is a different range and stays. `retired: true` is the id tombstone: it is written by a removal and by undoing a style step, it is sticky under merge (logical OR), and a retired id is never revived. Undoing a removal and redoing a style step both re-add the style under a fresh id at its own z, so the layer order comes back as it was. retired records keep shifting with the text, because those re-adds read their offsets.
rejected: A clear alone: the record stays alive on the peer's offsets, so a clear carried by a different diff path lands one character off at a repeated character and a sliver of the removed range shows
Retiring only records the removal fully covers: a partly covered record stays alive on the peer's offsets, so the same sliver shows at its outer edge
decisions.reason: With no common ancestor, reconcile can only tell removal from not-yet-seen by a record that is present. A clear or a retired record is that record, and an id is the one thing a diff cannot misplace.

decisions.topic: Known limit: the remaining edge of a carried removal
decisions.choice: A record a removal touched never shows again, whichever way a diff resolves a repeated character, because it is out by id. Exactly three things remain, and each needs a race. (1) The boundary between a clear and its kept part is placed by one diffText between the remover's text and the winning text. If the winning side changed a run of repeated characters or a repeated substring at that boundary, the kept part can sit to one side of where the keystrokes put it, or lose characters, by up to the amount of text the winning side added or removed there. (2) A clear hides a record its author had not seen, such as a colour made in the same race or another client's kept part, by position only. If that record and the clear reached the winning text by different paths, and the winning side changed repeated text at the clear's edge, that record can show beside the clear by the same amount. (3) If one client undoes a style step while another partly removes the same range, the kept part stays, because undo writes no clear.
decisions.reason: The person asked at Gate 2 to close this or state it. Case 1 cannot be closed from text alone: repeated characters have no identity and reconcile sees no keystrokes. Cases 2 and 3 concern records the remover never saw, so they cannot be retired by id.

decisions.choice: While shouldDiscardRemoteElement drops a remote update because the local user edits that element (also while resizing or creating it), the update's text and every non-range field are discarded as today. Its ranges are NOT discarded: reconcileElements calls mergeTextRanges(local, remote), so each of its records, including clears and retired flags, joins the local element at once, mapped onto the local text, keeping the local version and nonce. The preview redraws from the scene update, and offsets address the text in the editor, so nothing is stale. Local records win position over remote for any id they hold natively. When editing ends nothing special runs: the local version is broadcast as usual if typing bumped it, and the next delivery of either version merges through the ordinary path to the same element on both clients, whichever wins on version. The discard branch never bumps, and a tie after editing ends takes Collab's bump as any equal-version race does.
rejected: Holding the dropped update aside and replaying it at submit: it needs local state outside the element, which NFR-3 rules out of the merge
Bumping the version at submit past the dropped update: it changes reconcile for no range reason and elements with no ranges must reconcile as today
decisions.reason: reconcileElements keeps its signature and stays pure, and FR-21's three demands are met by the same merge as FR-19.

decisions.choice: textRanges is never written straight from a delta. ElementsDelta.applyDelta calls applyTextRangesDelta, which starts from the element's current records, shifts them to the delta's text if the delta holds originalText, then applies the difference between the delta's two sides by id: an id alive in the delta's deleted side and not in its inserted side is retired; an id alive in the inserted side and not in the deleted side is re-added, under a fresh id at its own z if its current record is retired. Offsets from a delta are used only when that delta also restores originalText and the element's current text equals the delta's deleted text, or when a record is collapsed on both the element and the delta's deleted side and the delta's inserted ranges address the resulting text, which is how undoing the step that lost a word brings its range back too. Undoing a range step after a remote text edit therefore keeps offsets on the current text. Undo and redo are forward operations: they merge with peers like any edit.
rejected: Replacing textRanges from the delta: a peer's union would bring an undone record back, and offsets would go stale after an interleaved remote text edit
decisions.reason: Delta applies only the keys it holds, so a separate range key must be reconciled with the current text at apply time.

decisions.topic: Known limit: undo after a same-version merge
decisions.choice: StoreSnapshot detects change by a rising version (store.ts:935), so a merge that keeps the version does not refresh the store snapshot. That is the client whose own element won, or who is editing, resizing or creating it, in reconcile's discard branch. A client that took the remote has a rising version, through the winner's higher version or Collab's bump, and its snapshot is current, so the limit does not reach it. On the discard-branch client, the next local edit's history step also spans records carried in by that merge. Undoing that one step retires those records, and a range a peer removed in that merge shows again, under a fresh id. Offsets stay valid and clients still converge. No workaround is written; packages/element/src/store.ts is outside the allowlist.
decisions.reason: A merge must not raise a version inside reconcile (NFR-3). The limit needs a race the local element won, then a local edit, then an undo of that exact step.

decisions.topic: Known limit: overlap is not repaired at restore
decisions.choice: Overlap between stored records is not malformed (FR-18). It stays as stored, in memory, in files and on the wire, and only getTextStyleRuns resolves it, by the fixed layer order. A saved element can therefore hold records that no character shows.
decisions.reason: Overlap is the normal output of FR-4 and of merging. Flattening it would rewrite join state.

decisions.topic: Known limit: deleted text in origin.text
decisions.choice: A carried record's origin names the losing version's full text. An element stores each distinct such text once, in the highest record that carries it, and every other record that carries it points to that record with textFrom. So after a concurrent-edit race text deleted on one client can stay in that element, in memory, in saves and on the wire, until the next style action or text edit on that element: one copy per losing text, not one per record. Only a race writes it: a merge sets origin only when the base does not hold the id or holds it carried. A deletion with no race keeps the record collapsed and native, so it leaves no old text in the element on either client.
decisions.reason: Carrying needs the register's own text, and any local edit drops it. This matches the PII line in requirements.md.

decisions.topic: One copy of each register text (NFR-2, FR-19, NFR-3)
decisions.choice: A merge stores each distinct register text once per container. shareOriginTexts runs last in mergeTextRanges, over the canonical records. Walking from the highest (z, id) down, the first record with a given text keeps { version, versionNonce, text, start, end }, and every later record with that text gets { version, versionNonce, textFrom: <that record's id>, start, end }. The highest holds it because the MAX_TEXT_RANGES cap cuts from the lowest, so a kept record's holder is never cut. getOriginTexts reads a container's holders into a Map by id, and getRegister resolves textFrom through it, so every step of a merge still works on whole registers. Nothing else changes: record count, ids, offsets, retired and every register are what they would be if each record held its own copy. sanitizeTextRanges keeps an inline origin as before, and keeps a textFrom only if, after the cap, it names a record of that container whose own origin holds text at least as long as the origin's end; otherwise the origin goes and the record stays, as with any invalid origin. A textFrom never points at another textFrom. areTextRangesEqual compares text with text and textFrom with textFrom, and a held origin never equals a shared one. The local paths need nothing new: a style action and a text edit drop every origin; applyTextRangesDelta keeps records and ids while the text is unchanged, retires by copy, and its cap also cuts from the lowest. The bound: the origin text stored in an element is at most the sum of its distinct register texts, of which there are at most 1,024, and every one of them was delivered whole in some version, so a merge can no longer store more text than it received. No record is past that bound and nothing is dropped: an element keeps every record, offset and register, and one copy of each distinct text. Measured on the scratch copy with the security review's two deliveries through real restore and reconcile, 1,024 native records, JSON.stringify of the result. 2,000 characters: 71,634 bytes delivered, 149,918 serialised, was 2,186,711. 100,000: 463,636 delivered, 443,918 serialised, was 102,734,710. 520,000: 2,143,637 delivered, 1,712,110 serialised, was 533,662,903. 540,000: 2,223,636 delivered, 1,772,110 serialised, where JSON.stringify threw RangeError: Invalid string length. 700,000: 2,863,632 delivered, 2,252,110 serialised. An element can still grow by what is delivered to it, up to one distinct text per record, as it can by a long text with no ranges at all.
rejected: A per-element cap on origin.text length in (z, id) order: a record's length comes from its register and a newer register can be shorter, so a cut at an intermediate merge can differ from a cut at the end and arrival order shows. An ordinary race of 200 records on a 20,000-character note also hits any cap small enough to help, and past it a record loses its origin or its styling
A text table on the container with an index in every origin: every origin changes shape, and three existing tests pin origin.text on a carried record
Packing in sanitizeTextRanges as well: a message with 1,024 inline copies stores what it delivered and multiplies nothing, a merge packs it, and valid input still comes back as the same object
decisions.reason: The security review showed 2.1 MB delivered serialising to 534 MB, and 540,000 characters throwing in JSON.stringify, because the cap bounds records and each record wrote the whole text. All of that growth is duplicates, so removing the duplicates removes it with no loss. FR-19 and NFR-3 hold with no new argument: packing is a pure function of the merged records, applied after every decision of the merge, so two clients with the same records store the same container, whatever order they reached them in. No copy of this code is released, and earlier files of this run hold inline origins, which stay valid, so nothing migrates.

decisions.topic: Known limit: convergence waits for the next delivery
decisions.choice: FR-19 holds once each client has received the other's latest version, not at the moment of a race. No client ever shows stale offsets meanwhile. Until then a bumped client differs from the other in version, versionNonce and updated, and if only one direction was delivered, the receiver holds merged records the sender lacks. Neither sends anything because of that. The next delivery is that client's next broadcast of any scene change, the full sync that follows a broadcast (SYNC_FULL_SCENE_INTERVAL_MS, 20 s, queued only by a broadcast), or a Firebase save by either client, which reconciles the stored scene back in. No timer forces one, so a quiet room stays in that state. Firebase: isSavedToFirebase compares the sum of versions, so a merge with no version rise does not make that client save. A client that took a remote element has a higher sum and saves, and saveToFirebase's own reconcileElements merges against the stored scene. So the stored scene lacks a merged record only if that client left before its throttled save ran, and then the winner's next version rise stores it.
decisions.reason: excalidraw-app/** does not change, and these are today's delivery rules for every element.

decisions.choice: Ctrl+Z inside the textarea is the browser's own, because App's key handler bails inside a writable element. It changes text only, and FR-16 treats that as any other edit: a colour applied in the session is not undone by it, and a word it brings back stays unstyled, because that word's record stays collapsed. The app's undo after leaving the editor restores text and ranges together.
decisions.reason: The textarea stays (FR-15), and its undo stack is not ours to change.

decisions.topic: Known limit: canvas bidi model and Arabic shaping
decisions.choice: On a line with a visible run, layoutTextLine splits the line into ltr and rtl segments by a simple strong-character model, not the full Unicode bidi algorithm, so a mixed-direction line can place runs differently from the same unstyled line. Each canvas piece is its own fillText, so a run boundary inside an Arabic word breaks letter joining at that boundary. SVG text keeps one <text> per line, so the browser shapes and orders it, but SVG highlight rects use the same layout. Lines with no visible run take today's path, with context.direction set back to the element's direction, because the line before may have left a piece's direction on the context.
decisions.reason: The canvas has no API for shaping across fillText calls, and jsdom cannot test a fuller model.

decisions.topic: Known limit: the compact panel's Background title
decisions.choice: The highlight picker has type elementBackground, and Picker.tsx titles its popup by type when showTitle is set, which ColorPicker does in compact mode. So in the compact and mobile panels the open popup reads "Background". The trigger's title and aria-label are right. Picker.tsx is outside the allowlist.
decisions.reason: A cosmetic label in one mode, and the scope cannot change in this run.

decisions.choice: MAX_TEXT_RANGES = 1024 records per element, counting retired, clear, collapsed and kept-part records. canonicalizeTextRanges keeps the highest (z, id), so past the cap the lowest layers are dropped, identically on every client, and that styling disappears. Records never leave the list otherwise, and a removal adds its clear plus up to two kept parts per touched record, so a heavily restyled element reaches the cap sooner than its visible runs suggest. A dropped record cannot return from a peer, because the merged list is cut the same way. This cap bounds records, not bytes; One copy of each register text is what bounds the text they hold.
decisions.reason: NFR-2 needs a bound on stored records, and a grow-only list has no other.

decisions.topic: Text diff mechanism (FR-3, FR-16, FR-19, NFR-2, NFR-3, Gate 4)
decisions.choice: diffText no longer fills a table and no longer falls back at a cell cap; MAX_DIFF_CELLS is gone. Everything is in packages/element/src/textDiff.ts, and diffText stays the one function shiftTextRanges and mergeTextRanges share. It searches before it trims. A queue of gaps starts with the two whole texts. Each gap takes its longest common run of at least MIN_MATCH_LENGTH (3) characters, which splits it into a left and a right gap, breadth-first. An index of oldText's 3-character grams finds the runs: a flat Int32Array table sized to the text, not a Map. In a gap the search starts at the middle of the gap's new text and moves outward, so that of runs of equal length the one nearest the middle wins and a repetitive note splits in half each time. It steps by the best length so far minus 1, because a longer run must hold a whole gram at one of those positions. At each position it tries at most MAX_MATCH_CANDIDATES (16) old positions, nearest the gap's own diagonal first. The longer of the common prefix and common suffix is the first gap's starting best, so a run must be strictly longer to beat it: a tie stays where trimming put it, and a change that repeats text beside it behaves as before. When the search ends, only the first and last gaps are trimmed of a common prefix and suffix, which keeps short matches at the text's two ends as before. A change of fewer than MIN_MATCH_LENGTH characters in total skips the search and goes straight to the final pass, so typing one character costs the trim and one work unit. A block never starts or ends inside a surrogate pair. Every step charges a DiffMeter, and when the meter runs out the search stops and keeps what it has found (see Diff budget per merge). Repeated text has no identity: when two copies of a run are equally long, a range follows the one this search reaches first, and only the person typing knows which copy they meant. The hunks the search leaves then go through refineHunks, the final diff pass, which has its own decision below.
rejected: Raising the cell cap: the second cause is under the cap, so a larger cap does nothing for it
Myers or any other minimal edit script: a minimal script still matches the original's letters inside added text, so runs fragment and the anchor is lost
Tokenising into words first: generated text has no words, and the brief needs both
Anchoring only on grams unique to both texts: repeated lines and repeated paragraphs have none
Scanning each gap left to right: on tied runs it peels one block per pass, so repeated lines spend the budget one line at a time
Sliding only the first and last hunks after a trim: a word of two letters left after the trim cannot anchor, so "Bid" to "Before Bid after" still loses the word
A Map as the gram index: it was slower per reconcile on the forged element than a flat Int32Array table
decisions.reason: There are three causes, not two, and this covers all of them. First, a cell cap fell back to one hunk once the two changes were far apart. Second, the eager backtrack matched the original's letters inside added text, the runs fragmented, and MIN_MATCH_LENGTH dropped them. Third: a common prefix or suffix took letters the addition shares with the word, so the insertion landed inside the word and the range widened over the added text. Searching before trimming closed that only where the suffix run beats the prefix run or the word is the whole text, as in "Bid" to "Before Bid". The Gate 4 review found it still open on "foo Bid" to "foo Before Bid", and getSlide in the final diff pass is what closes it. All figures here are from the final code, on a scratch bundle under node, never on a project file, and were run again on the scratch copy of this round's fixes with the same fixtures: each came out the same, because diffText's output changes only for a change of under MIN_MATCH_LENGTH characters. A word changed at each end at 1,010, 1,100 and 1,500 characters keeps every word (162 of 162, 177 of 177, 243 of 243). Tab on all lines of 468, 1,054 and 1,407 characters keeps every word (82, 182 and 243). U30 pins Tab at 1,054 and 1,407 and Shift+Tab at 1,126 and 1,503 through the real editor, on prose, and the same on digits at 1,061, 1,415, 1,133 and 1,511. 100 and 333 characters on each side of the label keep all 4 words; 333 on each side of the 326-character paragraph keeps all 53. mapTextSpan(digits.slice(5000, 5100), digits, 10, 20) is { start: 5010, end: 5020 }. Scripted random edits, 66 cells of prose, code and list text from 800 to 30,000 characters with 3 to 100 edits and six kinds of edit, 25 trials each: of 3,523,451 words no edit touched, at least 99.91% land exactly in every cell. Over all cells 144 land on another copy of the same word, 30 widen over a repeated word, 19 collapse and 2 land elsewhere. 20,000 fuzzed cases, half with emoji: hunks always rebuild the new text and stay in order, and no hunk edge falls inside a surrogate pair. The work is a pure function of the two texts and the meter, and uses no clock, randomness or module state (NFR-3). Work follows repetition, and past the budget Tab loses words, as the Known limit on the budget records: 100,016 characters of unique lines used 1,868,676 units in 10.9 ms and kept all 1,785 lines, and 1,000 of one 19-character line (19,999 characters) used 1,209,258 units and kept all 1,000, but 1,000 of one 75-character line (74,999 characters) kept 8 of 1,000.

decisions.topic: Final diff pass: refineHunks (FR-3, FR-16, FR-19, Gate 4 review)
decisions.choice: refineHunks in packages/element/src/textDiff.ts is the last step of diffText. It was added after the Gate 4 review, from that review's two major findings. It was not in this plan's earlier design. It fixes two defects, and the Gate 4 round 2 review found the second still open on the path that matters most: a keystroke returned before the pass, so typing the addition one character at a time left the first character inside the word, the range widened by one, and every later keystroke was strictly inside it. First, a kept token with no 3-character anchor collapsed: "OK" to "Not OK at all", "v2" to "release v2 now", and Tab on a note of one-character lines. Second, an addition beside a word landed inside it and the range widened over the added text: "foo Bid" to "foo Before Bid" styled "Before Bid". When it runs: on the hunks the search leaves, on the trimmed hunk when the search found no block, on the trimmed hunk when either text is under MIN_MATCH_LENGTH characters, and on the trimmed hunk of a change of under MIN_MATCH_LENGTH characters in total, which is what a keystroke is. It does not run for equal texts, or when the meter cannot pay for the index, because those return first. First loop, over the hunks: a hunk passes through when meter.left <= 0 or when either of its sides is empty. Otherwise it charges oldLength + newLength, once, and tries alignLines, then alignToken. alignLines needs both sides of the hunk to hold the same number of lines, at least 2. It gives one hunk per line pair, trimmed at both ends, so a one-character line keeps its place on Tab. alignToken needs an old side of 1 or 2 characters that is not all whitespace, has a word edge on both sides, and sits against a longer new side. It takes the first copy of that token in the new side with a word edge on both sides and no split surrogate pair, and replaces the hunk with the two insertions around that copy. Hunks empty on both sides are then dropped. Second loop, over what is left: a pure insertion or deletion, while meter.left > 0, charges its own length once and calls getSlide, and every other hunk is left alone. getSlide does nothing unless the hunk's place in the other text is inside a word. Otherwise it tries one step left, then one step right, up to the hunk's length, moving only while the text repeats and only inside the neighbouring hunks, and takes the first place outside a word that splits no surrogate pair. A word character is /[\p{L}\p{N}]/u tested on one UTF-16 unit, so an astral letter does not count as one. Past the budget neither loop does anything: the lines of a gap the search never reached are not aligned, which is why Tab loses them, and a short change keeps the hunk the trim gave. Typing was checked through the real editor, one input event per character: Before and Xefore typed in front of a coloured Bid, and escalation typed in front of a coloured engineer, leave the word alone; typing inside a word extends it; typing after it leaves it alone. The one typed case that stays wrong has its own Known limit below.
decisions.reason: Both defects hit an ordinary edit with no race, on characters that are all still there, against FR-3. Each step is pure and charged to the one meter, so NFR-3 and the budget hold, and each does work linear in the hunk it was charged for. Taking the first word-edged copy and trying left before right make every result a fixed choice; repeated text has no identity, so no choice is more right than another. U28 and U30 pin both defects: "addition beside a word", "kept token with no 3-character anchor", and Tab on the 500-line, 200-line and five-line notes, and the typed path through the real editor.

decisions.topic: Known limit: a typed word that ends in the styled word's first letter (FR-3)
decisions.choice: The final pass moves an insertion only to a word edge of the old text. Typed directly in front of a styled word with no space first, a character equal to that word's first letter, after another word character, has no such edge: in thengineer the diff puts the new e after the shared one, strictly inside the range, so the range widens by one and every later keystroke at that caret extends it. Measured on the scratch copy, one character at a time: the plus a space typed before a coloured engineer at the start of a text styles e engineer; me plus a space before engineer in the engineer said styles e engineer; go plus a space before oops styles o oops; BoB plus a space before Bid styles B Bid. A doubled first letter does the same on its first keystroke, because a slide takes no more steps than the hunk is long: o plus a space before oops styles o oops. The unfixed code gave the same result or a wider one in each. The text is right and nothing is lost; the range covers the extra characters until the person restyles them. The person has not accepted this limit yet.
decisions.reason: diffText sees two strings, no range and no caret, and in these cases both readings give the same two strings, so no change inside it can tell them apart. Closing it takes the caret passed from the editor, or a range-aware slide in the mapping. Each changes the editor wiring or the contract of mapSpanThroughHunks, which this round's fix does not, so it goes back to the person.

decisions.choice: mergeTextRanges bounds its diff work per call with one work meter, which replaces the cell budget. textDiff.ts holds the only constant, MAX_DIFF_WORK, and textRangeMerge.ts repeats none of it: MAX_MERGE_DIFF_CELLS, DIFF_TEXT_MAX_CELLS and getCoarseHunk are removed, so the two files cannot disagree. Imports: `import { MAX_DIFF_WORK, diffText, mapSpanThroughHunks } from "./textDiff";` and `import type { DiffMeter, TextHunk } from "./textDiff";`. Order, unchanged from Gate 3: after allIds, `const survivors = canonicalizeTextRanges([...allIds].map((id) => (baseMap.get(id) ?? otherMap.get(id))!)).reverse();` and the loop is `for (const { id } of survivors)`, so records the MAX_TEXT_RANGES cap drops are gone before any diff runs, and the highest (z, id) is served first. Spend: before the loop, `const meter: DiffMeter = { left: MAX_DIFF_WORK };` and `const hunksByText = new Map<string, readonly TextHunk[]>();`. On a miss in hunksByText, `hunks = diffText(reg.text, base.originalText, meter);` and the result is stored under reg.text, so each distinct text is paid for once. diffText charges the meter for what it does, the final diff pass included, and stops when the meter runs out. A text it cannot pay to index costs nothing, so it does not stop a later, shorter one. The exception is an old text under MIN_MATCH_LENGTH characters, which reaches the final pass before that gate: alignToken scans the new side at about 40 ns per character, within the stated limit, and the security review's Low on it is left as it is. `const mapped = mapSpanThroughHunks(hunks, reg.start, reg.end);` follows as before. Test, in packages/excalidraw/tests/data/reconcile.textRanges.test.ts, counts work and never times it: `vi.mock("@excalidraw/element/textDiff", ...)` wraps diffText in a vi.fn over importOriginal, cleared just before the merge, so its calls and results are visible. W is 10,000 generated characters. The winner holds 1,024 carried records with distinct 100-character origins, L1 holds one record at a higher z whose origin is W.slice(5000, 5100) with offsets [10, 20), and L2 holds three records at a lower z whose ids sort first, with distinct 100-character origins. One merge makes exactly 1,024 diffText calls, the first on W.slice(5000, 5100) and none on an L2 origin. More than none and fewer than 1,024 of them return several hunks, and the last returns one, which shows the budget ran out. That record lands at [5010, 5020) in both arrival orders, both orders give the same element, merging L2 again returns the base object, and the lowest surviving record is collapsed with its origin kept. A second case carries a range across a change at each end of W to its true offsets.
rejected: Iterating all ids in sorted order: which records the cap has already dropped depends on arrival order, so a doomed record would spend budget on one client and not on another, and those clients would stop converging
Pricing a diff before it runs, by trimmed cells: the work no longer follows cells, and a text could only be served whole or not at all
A separate merge constant: a second number is the disagreement this round removes
A fixed price per text: a one-word edit would cost as much as a hostile text, and a fourth ordinary register would lose its diff
decisions.reason: Value: 2,000,000 work units for one merge, the same as for one local diff. The limit, with a and b the lengths of the two texts of one diffText call and n = min(a, b): that call takes the meter at most max(2n + 1, a + b - 1) below zero, which is at most a + b + 1. So one merge spends at most MAX_DIFF_WORK + a + b + 1, where a and b are those of the one diff the meter ran out on. This plan used to state MAX_DIFF_WORK + 2 * min + 2, which was wrong because it left out the final diff pass. Derivation from the code. The index is charged only when indexWork <= meter.left, so it leaves the meter at 0 or above. In the search every candidate is behind a read of meter.left > 0, and one candidate charges back + 1 + length, where back <= length <= n, so at most 2n + 1. From left >= 1 that leaves left >= -2n, and the second searchAt of that findLongestBlock turn charges 1 with no read before it, so the search ends at -(2n + 1) or higher. refineHunks reads meter.left before every charge, and a charge is the length of one hunk, at most a + b, so from left >= 1 it ends at -(a + b - 1) or higher. Past that one unit, nothing is charged once the meter is at or below zero: both refineHunks loops skip, and a later diff in the same merge has indexWork > 0 >= left, so it returns the trimmed hunk. So one charge crosses zero, in one diff. Proved by running it on the final code, old "0123456789" against new random letters. New 900,000: the meter ends at -729,136, from index 900,040, search 929,086, so 170,874 left when the final pass charges 900,010. Limit 900,011. New 800,000: -425,906, from index 800,040, search 825,856, so 374,104 left when the final pass charges 800,010. Limit 800,011. The old formula gave 22 for both. The overrun is linear and harmless: those two take about 10 ms. Tightest found, new 984,070: 984,062 against 984,081. 200,000 random pairs of short texts with random meters: none past max(2n + 1, a + b - 1), and none charged anything with the meter at or below zero. Outside the meter are the trim, at most 2n compares per distinct register text, so linear in the payload as before; sorting the blocks found, each of which cost at least 4 units; mapping each surviving record through its hunks, a binary search on oldEnd, 18 steps at each end for 169,000 hunks, the longest list measured, which gives the same output as the walk it replaced because hunks are sorted on oldEnd and oldStart never passes oldEnd (300,000 fuzzed diffs, 220,224,528 spans, 0 differences); and one Map lookup per carried record to store its text once. Measured on 115 adversarial inputs (random text over small alphabets, periodic text, blocks of 3 characters, no match at all), with old texts up to 400,000 characters, in three runs: the slowest took 30.9 to 33 ms (25,000 blocks of 3 characters), and the largest overrun past zero was 399,998 units (300,000 characters of period 3 against its reverse, limit 600,001). Forged-element timing, measured through real restoreElements and reconcileElements under jsdom: 1,024 records, about 254 KB of JSON, against a 10,000-character text, nine reconciles per fixture. Four text shapes, random letters, two letters, periodic text and repeated lines, each with two origin kinds, unrelated 100-character text and slices of the base. Re-measured on the scratch copy of this round's fixes with the same fixtures, three runs; each figure here is the higher of those runs and the earlier set. Median and worst single run in ms: random 21.7 and 31.6 unrelated, 10.1 and 12.0 slices; two letters 16.1 and 19.4 unrelated, 16.2 and 19.3 slices; periodic 14.2 and 16.6 unrelated, 12.2 and 14.0 slices; lines 15.8 and 18.5 unrelated, 10.3 and 12.1 slices. So medians run 10.1 to 21.7 ms and the worst single run was 31.6 ms. The security review's mapping fixture, 1,024 records at the end of a text of 100,000 to 169,000 changed lines, up to about 1 MB of JSON, took 269.1 ms median and 375.3 ms worst before the binary search and 12.8 to 23.1 ms median and 32.8 ms worst on the scratch copy, nine reconciles per fixture. Ten such elements in one message, 8.1 MB, took 2,458 ms before and 178 ms on the scratch copy. All of these scratch-copy timings need re-measuring on the typed code. In U28's budget scenario 44 of the 1,024 diffs return several hunks before the meter runs out. An ordinary race stays under the budget: three register texts of 10,000 characters with one edit each used 120,212 units on varied text and 273,677 on one paragraph repeated to that length. Convergence: a record native to the base and a register equal to the base are not mapped and cost nothing. Every other surviving record is remapped from its own register on every merge that reaches the loop, and a merge whose other side has no records returns the base and adds none. So nothing carries spend between calls: it depends only on the base text and the registers of the surviving records, not on how a client reached them. The survivors are the same on every client, because the top MAX_TEXT_RANGES by (z, id) of a union does not depend on the order of the unions, and the cut comes before any diff. The order they are served in comes from that same canonical sort, and a partial diff is a pure function of the two texts and what the meter holds on arrival, so the result is the same however a client reached those survivors. A bumped client's native records register the base's own text, which diffText answers with no work, so a bump changes no spend. Two clients with the same two versions compute the same element (NFR-3), and the merge stays idempotent: a repeat sees the same survivors and registers, gets the same hunks and returns the base. meter and hunksByText live and die in one call, so no local-only state enters the merge.

decisions.topic: Known limit: the diff budget is per element
decisions.choice: MAX_DIFF_WORK is per diffText call for a local text edit and per element for a merge, one mergeTextRanges call, so many forged elements still add up in proportion to payload size. What really happens past the budget: a change of under MIN_MATCH_LENGTH characters keeps the hunk the trim gave, with no slide; a diff that cannot pay for its index returns one hunk, the text between the common prefix and the common suffix, and a diff that runs out partway keeps every block it has found and leaves each remaining gap as a hunk. A range wholly inside such a hunk collapses and styles nothing: a carried range keeps its origin, so a later merge with budget left can still place it, and a native range stays collapsed as a deleted range does, until an app undo restores it. A range with one end inside the hunk keeps only its part outside the hunk. A range that spans the whole hunk keeps both ends and also covers the hunk's new text. In a merge the highest (z, id) records are served first, so the records that lose out are the lowest layers. A text over about 400,000 characters is never indexed, since the index alone would use the budget, so an edit to it behaves like the trim: one change is exact, and a range between two far-apart changes collapses. Tab reaches this limit, the person accepted that at Gate 4 for very long notes, and the loss is silent: nothing warns, and the word just stops being styled. The cliff depends on repetition and line length, not on one size. Measured on the final code, diffText from a scratch bundle, and run again on the scratch copy of this round's fixes with the same fixtures, which gave the same hunks, kept and lost counts and work. Tab on all lines, where kept means the word stays on its true offset. One line repeated (75 characters): fine at 30,000 characters; at 40,000, 448 of 534 lines lost; at 50,000, 640 of 667; at 100,000, 1,330 of 1,334. Lines differing only by a row number: fine at 30,000; at 40,000, 351 of 478 lost; at 100,000, 1,185 of 1,190. Ten lines repeated: fine at 50,000; at 60,000, 18 of 1,118 lost; at 80,000, 1,393 of 1,482 lost. All lines unique: fine at 100,000; at 150,000, 2,478 of 2,664 lost; at 200,000, 3,528 of 3,548. At about 400,000 characters nothing is indexed and all but one line is lost. Through the real editor in jsdom: Tab at 29,999 characters kept the word at its true offset; at 40,049 the record collapsed and styled nothing; one app undo restored it. Other edits on the one-line note: 20 scattered line edits lost 30 of 800 lines at 60,000 and 773 of 1,334 at 100,000. A change to the first and last lines held up to 200,000, the largest tested.
rejected: A budget across a whole reconcile: clients reconcile different batches and could stop converging
decisions.reason: The person asked at Gate 3 to record the remaining per-element limit. Convergence decides it: the bound must be a function of one element's two versions. At Gate 4 the person accepted the Tab limit on very long notes and asked for these numbers to be recorded. The search spends the budget on repeated lines first, so repetition sets the cliff: a 40,000-character note of one repeated line loses what a 100,000-character note of unique lines keeps.

decisions.topic: A diff of any line count returns (NFR-2)
decisions.choice: refineHunks pushes the hunks alignLines returns one at a time, in a for...of loop, so a hunk of any number of lines returns. It used to pass them to one aligned.push(...lines) call, and about 120,000 lines overflowed the call stack and threw RangeError out of diffText, so out of reconcileElements, shiftTextRanges and applyTextRangesDelta. aligned.push(...token) stays, because alignToken returns two hunks. Measured on the scratch copy through real restoreElements and reconcileElements under vitest, a native record against a text with every line changed, no origin needed: all 13 counts tried from 90,000 to 180,000 lines return, the former throwing range of 120,000 to 165,000 included, and a benign element sent in the same batch is applied. 100,000 lines also returns at 2,000 and 5,000 extra stack frames. From about 170,000 lines the search runs the meter out before the final pass, so the diff returns one hunk, as it did. U28 pins 150,000 lines: 150,000 hunks, ending on the true last hunk.
rejected: Catching the RangeError in the merge: a local edit and an undo reach it too, and a caught throw leaves the range unmapped
decisions.reason: Both reviews of Gate 4 round 2 rated this a blocker against NFR-2. It lands with the binary search in mapStart and mapEnd, because it raises the hunk count those read.

decisions.topic: Gate 4 round 2 review: units this round changes
decisions.choice: The sections describe the code as it will be once this round's fixes are typed. Every one of the 31 units stays. Eight change, each with real sites against its file as it now is: U01 (the shared origin type), U02 (the push loop, the keystroke's final pass, the binary search), U03 (getOriginTexts, the validator, equality), U04 (the non-string guard, registers through textFrom, shareOriginTexts), U11 (originalText in restore), U27, U28 and U30 (their tests). U28 also adds the rule 10 test, which stays as specified, and changes one expected value: spent 0 to spent 1 on the typed character, because a keystroke now runs the final pass. Every other test line stays. Dispatch them in that order, in one execute_batch: U03 depends on U01 and U02, U04 on U01, U02 and U03, U11 on U03, U27 on U03 and U11, U28 on U02, U03, U04 and U11, and U30 on U02 and U03. Each of the other 23 units keeps its behaviour, rules, exports, covers, depends_on and checks, and has one site: an anchor on line 1 of its file, whose rule says the unit is complete. That unit was typed before Gate 4, its file does not change this round, and its packet is not dispatched.
decisions.reason: The schema needs at least one site on an edit. Keeping every unit keeps every FR and AC covered and the whole plan readable, while the anchors state that nothing is asked of those units.

decisions.choice: sanitizeTextRanges(raw, originalText) is the single validator. restore.ts calls it, and every reader (getTextStyleRuns, the merge, the delta) calls it too, so bad data from any path is repaired or dropped and never thrown on. It drops the whole container when textHash does not match originalText (stale against the text, for example an older client edited the text). It drops any record with wrong types, an inverted span, or no usable attribute; removes an unusable colour attribute; clamps out-of-bounds offsets; and caps the list at MAX_TEXT_RANGES by keeping the highest (z, id). Valid input comes back as the same object. Overlap is not dropped at restore, because stored overlap is the normal output of FR-4 and of a merge and repairing it there would break merging: an overlap is resolved by the fixed layer order, so the renderer only ever receives disjoint runs. The validator does not look at the length of origin.text. A shared origin is validated as One copy of each register text states. restore.ts keeps originalText only when it is a string and otherwise uses text, and mergeTextRanges returns the base when either side's originalText is not a string, because reconcileElements is public and a host can call it without restore. Both checks are new this round: a non-string value used to reach diffText and throw out of reconcile from a 1.2 KB message. A string originalText behaves exactly as before, and an empty one still falls back to text.
rejected: Flattening overlap in restore: restoreElements runs on every remote element before reconcile, so it would rewrite join state and make merging path-dependent
decisions.reason: Validate at restore and render defensively, with one function for both.

decisions.choice: A range colour is valid when it is a string of at most 64 characters and colorToHex(value) is not null. Colours reach SVG through setAttribute and the preview through element.style only, never through markup strings. Applying a transparent colour is stored as null, so a user cannot make text invisible through a range. Colours get applyDarkModeFilter(value, isDark) on canvas, in SVG and in the preview, as strokeColor does.
decisions.reason: One rule shared by restore, renderers and the actions.

decisions.choice: With an empty selection, or with the element selected and not being edited, actionChangeStrokeColor behaves exactly as today: it sets strokeColor and ranges keep their own colour. The range path runs only when appState.editingTextElement is set and the textarea has a non-empty selection.
decisions.reason: The reading the person accepted at Gate 1.

decisions.choice: A whole-text selection sets strokeColor only when no run has its own colour; otherwise it applies as a range. A deliberate select-all on plain text therefore sets strokeColor, and text typed later takes that colour too. This rule is in actionChangeStrokeColor in packages/excalidraw/actions/actionProperties.tsx.
decisions.reason: The editor auto-selects all text when an element opens for editing (textWysiwyg.tsx:1324), and a colour pick with no selection of the user's own must keep working as today (FR-13). The person kept this rule at Gate 3.

decisions.choice: A new button labelled "Reset text color and highlight" (action resetTextStyle, eraser icon) shows in the styles panel beside the text highlight picker while a text element is edited. Clicking it returns the selected characters to the element's own colour and to no highlight. With an empty selection it does nothing. Choosing the transparent swatch in the highlight picker also removes only the highlight. Both count as removal for FR-19.
rejected: A No color swatch in the stroke picker: the stroke palette has no such entry and picking transparent is a colour for every other element
Picking the element's strokeColor by hand: the range would keep that colour after a later strokeColor change
decisions.reason: One visible control does both jobs of FR-14, and the stroke picker keeps its meaning.

decisions.choice: A new action changeTextHighlight renders a ColorPicker while a text element is edited, with type "elementBackground" for the background palette and a new optional prop popup="textHighlight" naming its popup. It needs no new ColorPickerType, because colorPickerUtils.ts is outside the allowlist, and `popup` lets it sit beside the background picker while a sticky note label is edited. With an empty selection it changes nothing.
decisions.reason: Two pickers sharing one openPopup value would open together.

decisions.choice: The <textarea> stays. Its selectionStart and selectionEnd are originalText offsets as they are, because editable.value is originalText. While the element has visible runs, a preview layer (class excalidraw-wysiwyg-preview) sits directly behind the textarea with the same box, font and wrapping, shows the full text with coloured and highlighted spans, and the textarea's own text is transparent with its caret in the element's colour. With no visible runs there is no preview node and the textarea styles are as today. The canvas paints the styling when editing ends, because the canvas skips the element being edited.
rejected: A contenteditable editor: out of scope for this run
decisions.reason: The After line needs the word to show in red while editing, and jsdom can drive a textarea.

decisions.choice: Renderers call getTextLineRuns(element), which aligns element.text with originalText without measuring. When it returns null the renderer's existing code runs untouched, so elements with no ranges paint and export byte-identically. Canvas: all highlights first as fillRect, then text as one fillText per piece with textAlign left at an explicit x. SVG: a highlight is a <rect> appended to the element's <g> before every <text>; a coloured run is a <tspan> with fill; a run with no colour is a plain text node; each line stays one <text> with today's attributes, so text-anchor and the browser's bidi still apply. A highlight rect spans the full line height. Range colour and highlight are paint-only and never reach measureText.
decisions.reason: A <tspan> carries a fill but no background, which Gate 0 accepted as a rect behind the text.

decisions.choice: Vitest unit and jsdom tests only, no browser check. Canvas is asserted by draw calls, because vitest-canvas-mock paints no pixels. Verification uses yarn test:typecheck, yarn test:code and yarn test:app --watch=false as three separate commands. Never yarn test:update, which rewrites snapshots and would hide a regression. No existing snapshot file changes (AC-13). Tests of the meter count work and never read a clock. The exact `spent` tests in U28 never reach the forward-scan charge at textDiff.ts:123: each pair has no common run, or a run the trim's seed already holds, so every candidate returns at the bestLength check. The test in U28's last rule pins that charge. Removing the charge at textDiff.ts:99, :149, :496 or :405 fails at least 3 tests. The slide charge at textDiff.ts:432 has no test that fails when it is removed, and this round plans none.
decisions.reason: Run decisions from the brief and Gate 0, answer 2.

decisions.choice: The entry goes under Unreleased in packages/excalidraw/CHANGELOG.md with no PR link and no PR number. Never invent one.
decisions.reason: No PR exists yet, and the brief forbids an invented number.
